title: The database schema and migrations
request: PostgreSQL only, for a team of about 1,000 users, runnable locally and later in the cloud. Build the schema and migrations and a PostgreSQL implementation of the 9.1 storage interfaces, tested against a real database, never a mock.
spec: SQLAlchemy 2 models and Alembic migrations; documents read whole as JSON columns, what lists filter or sort on as indexed columns; append-only logs with a sequence per parent; immutable stage records; DCLAB_DATABASE_URL switches the product; a pooled connection; no raw SQL from request input. Done when the whole suite and make product-e2e pass against PostgreSQL and the projects list stays fast with 10,000 projects (measured, with the query plan).
plan: Ask the owner before touching the local PostgreSQL server: create two new databases (dclab_dev for working data, dclab_test for the tests, which empty it) and install the psycopg driver.

Write the schema: ten tables (workspace, app_user, membership, project, stage_record, activity, transition, draft, draft_event, intern_session) and the first migration; python -m dclab_rnd.storage upgrade.
Share the 'new document' builders between the file and PostgreSQL stores so both create identical documents.
Write the PostgreSQL stores: row locks for update, draft event numbers from an UPDATE of the draft row, the agent turn as an advisory lock, every query filtered by workspace.
Write one contract test that runs the same behaviours against both backends.
Switch the server with DCLAB_DATABASE_URL; run the whole suite on PostgreSQL and on files, and make product-e2e on PostgreSQL.
Measure a page of 50 projects among 10,000 with timings and the query plan; add a test that the migration and the models describe the same database; add make test-pg.

decisions.decision: Two fixed databases on the developer's machine: dclab_dev and dclab_test.
decisions.why: The tests empty their database; sharing one with working data would delete the owner's projects on every test run. A temporary database per run needs create and drop rights and can leave strays after a crash. The owner asked why two and agreed.

decisions.decision: A document read whole is JSONB; what a list filters or sorts on is a column with an index.
decisions.why: Stage records, solutions and drafts are always read whole, while lists need indexed workspace, status and time columns to stay fast at thousands of projects.

decisions.decision: Keep the file stores and switch with one setting.
decisions.why: Both backends stay tested by the same suite and contract test, and a laptop without PostgreSQL still runs.

decisions.decision: Each workspace folder is one workspace until accounts exist.
decisions.why: Accounts come in 10.2; until then the folder is the only identity a request has, and isolation can already be tested per workspace.

change: dclab_rnd/storage gained models.py (ten tables), db.py (engine, pool, migrations), postgres.py (projects, drafts and sessions on PostgreSQL behind the 9.1 Protocols), open_stores choosing the backend from DCLAB_DATABASE_URL, the first Alembic migration and the upgrade command. The file stores share their document builders with the PostgreSQL stores. Tests: test_storage_contract (one set of behaviours on both backends), test_storage_postgres (migration and models agree, a downgrade and upgrade round trip). make test-pg runs the suite on PostgreSQL. requirements gained psycopg.

findings.defect: Saving an intern session over another workspace's id was not refused on PostgreSQL.
findings.scenario: Workspace B saves a session whose id belongs to workspace A: the contract test expected KeyError, none was raised, and the row stayed A's while B believed it had saved.
findings.cause: The upsert's ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE workspace matched no row, but the driver reported rowcount -1, so the check 'rowcount == 0' never fired.
findings.fix: The upsert returns the saved id (RETURNING); no id back means the row belongs to another workspace, and save raises KeyError.
findings.impact: Workspace B was told its session was saved while nothing was written and the row stayed A's, so B lost its work without an error; the isolation between workspaces rested on a check that could never fire.

findings.defect: A stage record holding a score that is not a number was refused by the file store but stored as null by PostgreSQL.
findings.scenario: write_stage with score NaN: the file store raised ValueError (strict JSON); the PostgreSQL store's lenient encoder wrote null, so the same defect was hidden on one backend.
findings.cause: The PostgreSQL store encoded records with a helper that turned NaN into null.
findings.fix: Stage records are encoded strictly on both backends (allow_nan=False): a non-number score is a defect to surface, not to store.
findings.test: test_storage_contract: test_stage_records asserts ValueError and that no stage was written.
findings.impact: A stage that produced a NaN score was refused on a laptop with files but stored with a null score on PostgreSQL, so the same defect would surface in development and hide in the team deployment, where a stage with no score could pass for a finished one.

findings.defect: The 'newest change first' contract test failed now and then on the file store.
findings.scenario: Two projects created and updated within the same second: the file store sorts by an ISO time with one-second precision, so the order between them was arbitrary; four of five repeated runs failed.
findings.cause: The file store's timestamps have one-second precision.
findings.fix: The test waits just over a second between the two changes.
findings.impact: The contract test failed at random, four runs in five, so a red result would soon be read as noise and a real ordering bug in either backend could hide behind it.
findings.open: The file store still orders two changes made within the same second arbitrarily; only the test steps around it.

findings.defect: Three page tests failed on PostgreSQL though the product was right.
findings.scenario: test_pages_ops and test_pages_learn built file stores themselves and wrote files into their folders; with DCLAB_DATABASE_URL set the server read the database, so the jobs list lacked stage, intern and data entries and a pack count was 0 instead of 1.
findings.cause: The tests seeded data by writing store files directly instead of going through the stores the server uses.
findings.fix: The tests open their stores with open_stores, so seeding goes to the same backend the server reads; the project log gained an at= argument so tests can seed times through it.
findings.test: The whole suite passes on both backends (347 tests each).
findings.impact: Three page tests failed on PostgreSQL though the product was right; tests that seed by writing files check the file backend while claiming to check the database, so a real PostgreSQL defect on those pages would have gone unseen.

measurements.name: projects list at 10,000 projects
measurements.gate: The projects list stays fast with 10,000 projects, measured with the query plan (the package's Done when).
measurements.result: A page of 50 takes about 1 ms and uses the workspace index; reading one project takes 0.5 ms.
measurements.next: Page the /api/projects route itself (10.1 gave every route its models; paging stayed open).
measurements.against_gate: The gate asks that the projects list stays fast at 10,000 projects, with the query plan. A page of 50 takes about 1 ms and uses the workspace index, and reading one project takes 0.5 ms. The gate names no time limit, so 'fast' is read from these figures and the plan.
limits: Measured on the developer's machine with a local database and no other load; a shared server under many users will differ.
The /api/projects route itself was not paged yet, so the measured query is not what the page called at the time.
The projects were made for the measurement; documents of real size may read slower.

measurements.name: results unchanged by the storage backend
measurements.gate: The whole suite and make product-e2e pass on PostgreSQL with the same results as on files.
measurements.result: 347 tests pass on files and on PostgreSQL; the end-to-end flows give the same scores on both (0.8503 and 12.0954).
measurements.next: One earlier test run was very slow (110 s) with one error; eight repeats did not reproduce it, so it was reported as unexplained rather than hidden.
measurements.against_gate: The gate asks for the whole suite and make product-e2e to pass on PostgreSQL with the same results as on files. 347 tests pass on files and on PostgreSQL, and the end-to-end flows give the same scores on both (0.8503 and 12.0954): it passes.
limits: Equal scores on the end-to-end flows show storage does not change those results; they say nothing about model quality, since the flows run in quick mode.
One earlier run was very slow with a single error and did not reproduce; it stays unexplained, not ruled out.
Both backends ran on the same machine; several app instances sharing one database were not part of this check.

outcome: Done: projects, drafts and intern sessions run on PostgreSQL when DCLAB_DATABASE_URL is set, with ten tables and migrations, row and advisory locks that hold across processes, and tested workspace isolation. Tables and exports stayed files (9.3); old workspaces were not imported yet (9.4).
lessons: Do not trust rowcount after an upsert with a WHERE clause; ask the database for the row it wrote.
Run one contract test against both backends: it found two places where they disagreed.
Tests that seed data by writing a store's files bypass the backend under test; seed through the store.
Report a failure that does not reproduce as unexplained; do not drop it.
risks: Tests that empty their database would delete the owner's projects if they shared it with working data.
An upsert guarded by a WHERE clause can look successful when it wrote nothing.
Two backends can disagree silently (strict against lenient JSON) unless one contract test runs on both.
A lock held in one process means nothing to another: updates, draft event numbers and agent turns need locks in the database.
Lists that filter or sort inside JSON documents slow down at thousands of projects without indexed columns.
